=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter
Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of
Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and
look forward to your mark-up.
SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)
Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims
is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.
Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and
only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the
basket is recoverable.
Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after
Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims
unless expressly stated otherwise.
Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same
caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.
Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and
non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.
Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public
registers (see Disclosure Letter).
Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the
Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or
public records.
Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller
will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the
counterparty's written consent.
Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding)
will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.
Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing
bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds
flow.)
Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio
matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.
Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter
and is not expected to be material.
Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course
operating costs.
Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime
above.
Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.
Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and
records are fictional.
1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the
indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including
DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly
searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific
disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent,
payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.
2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause
11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final
written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.
3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2.
As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security
is included.
4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of
every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of
non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.
5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject
to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft
Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or
on-costs apply.
6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external
email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity
timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised
person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation
remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no
loss amount.
7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as
a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.
8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each
(AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether
each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.
9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale
consent is required merely because shares are sold.
10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of
the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the
Buyer has completed its own verification.
11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer
must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

## Overall assessment

**The Seller’s package materially favours the Seller.** It combines broad disclosure and deemed Buyer knowledge with narrow recovery rights—and leaves important completion risks unresolved. Wattlebridge could acquire those risks while losing the ability to recover for them.

Our baseline remains **100% of Paperbark Analytics for AUD 24 million, debt-free/cash-free, under NSW law**. Disclosure is not acceptance of a risk, proof that it has been resolved, or agreement to change that bargain.

This review is based on the supplied extracts; the underlying SPA, DD documents and funds flow need checking before final drafting.

## 1. Completion and price protections: highest priority

### Bluefen: consent alone is insufficient  
**Clauses 3 / 6.3; Disclosure Letter §2; DD-002**

Bluefen represents approximately **30% of FY26 revenue**. The Seller says consent is “addressed”, but its own disclosure confirms that no final written consent or evidence of satisfaction of associated conditions has been provided.

**Push back:**
- Make effective Bluefen consent a condition precedent for the Buyer’s benefit, waivable only by the Buyer.
- Require satisfaction of the relevant clause 11.3 conditions—not merely delivery of a consent letter.
- Require consent to cover this transaction and remain effective at Completion, without adverse amendments, fees or other conditions unless the Buyer approves them.
- Include a long-stop date and termination right if the condition fails.

A reasonable-endeavours obligation governs the Seller’s efforts; it does **not** substitute for the required outcome. Do not let “delivery” automatically deem the condition satisfied.

### Riverlark: no post-Completion release gap  
**Clauses 2 / 7; Disclosure Letter §3; DD-003**

Approximately **AUD 3.2 million** remains outstanding, and neither repayment nor final security discharge is evidenced. A promise to provide a release after Completion leaves the Buyer owning a company with unresolved debt/security exposure.

**Push back:**
- Obtain a lender payoff statement covering principal, interest, fees and all secured liabilities.
- Repay the facility through the completion funds flow, with binding lender release arrangements effective upon receipt of payment.
- Cover all relevant security, guarantees and registrations; require prompt evidence of registration removals where those necessarily follow settlement.
- Address change-control requirements pending repayment.
- Ensure the debt reduces the amount payable to the Seller under the agreed debt-free/cash-free mechanics, **without double counting** repayment and the price adjustment.

The Buyer should not pay AUD 24 million to the Seller and separately fund undiscounted acquisition debt.

### Completion bonuses: capture the full cost  
**Funds flow; Disclosure Letter §5; DD-005**

The **AUD 420,000** bonuses are conditional on Completion and continued employment. That does not establish that they are legally payable by the Seller rather than the Company. Omitting them from the funds flow risks leaving the Buyer with the cost.

**Push back:**
- Confirm the employing/paying entity, beneficiaries, payment timing and precise conditions.
- Allocate the agreed transaction-related cost to the Seller, through payment, a price deduction or a funded retention.
- Include applicable superannuation, payroll tax and other on-costs after verification.
- Prevent double counting through working capital, debt-like items and transaction expenses.

If obligations remain with the Company after Completion, a statement that they are “a matter for the Seller” is inadequate: require an enforceable funding and reimbursement mechanism.

### Ironquay: secure ownership, not merely payment protection  
**Clause 11.1; Disclosure Letter §4; DD-004 / DD-010**

The documents indicate that transfer of SOW3 Project Materials depends on cleared payment of **every SOW3 fee**. The AUD 180,000 open balance is a warning, not conclusive proof of non-payment. Equally, there is no evidence that the transfer condition has been met.

**Push back:**
- Reconcile all SOW3 fees and obtain payment evidence and Ironquay’s confirmation of the position.
- Require effective assignment/confirmation of all relevant rights and appropriate releases at or before Completion.
- Review the wider IP ownership chain and relevant third-party rights.
- Expand the specific indemnity beyond the invoice amount to cover reasonably attributable ownership/use disputes, claims, cure costs and associated loss, subject to negotiated scope.
- Keep that indemnity outside the general warranty basket, disclosure defence and general cap/time limit.

Paying an invoice—or indemnifying its amount—does not necessarily cure defective ownership of commercially important IP.

## 2. Liability regime: preserve meaningful recourse

### General cap, thresholds and time limits  
**Clauses 12.1–12.3 / 13**

The proposed **20% cap (AUD 4.8 million)**, **AUD 25,000 de minimis**, **AUD 250,000 deductible basket** and **18-month notification period** cumulatively transfer substantial risk to the Buyer.

**Recommended negotiating position:**
- Seek a higher general warranty cap, assessed against diligence findings and available recovery security.
- Reduce the de minimis and basket; seek a **tipping basket**, so qualifying claims become recoverable in full once the threshold is crossed.
- Aggregate connected claims when applying thresholds, preventing one underlying problem being fragmented into smaller claims.
- Seek a longer general warranty period—**24 months as an opening position**.
- Ensure timely notification preserves a claim even if its amount is not yet ascertainable; resist overly technical notice requirements and unduly short proceedings deadlines.

These protections must be assessed together, not as isolated concessions.

### Do not put every Claim into the general warranty regime  
**Fundamental/title; clauses 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5; tax/IP**

Applying limitations to “all Claims of any nature” could restrict payment obligations, completion undertakings, specific indemnities and other contractual remedies—not just warranty claims.

Require an express claims matrix:

| Claim category | Buyer position |
|---|---|
| General warranties | Separately negotiated cap, thresholds and survival period |
| Capacity, title and share encumbrances | No de minimis/basket; materially higher cap, at least purchase-price level as a negotiating position; longer survival |
| Pre-Completion tax | Dedicated tax indemnity/covenant, separate limitations and survival aligned with relevant assessment/review periods plus a notification buffer |
| Known-risk indemnities | Bespoke scope, cap and duration; not defeated by disclosure or Buyer knowledge |
| Payment, debt discharge and completion obligations | Not automatically constrained by warranty limitations |
| Fraud, fraudulent concealment and other non-excludable liability | Express carve-outs; no contractual protection for the Seller’s own fraud |

IP should not simply be declared “settled”. Distinguish general IP warranties from the identified Ironquay risk and negotiate meaningful protection for each.

Also preserve appropriate termination, injunctive and specific-performance rights. Any statutory liability exclusions require NSW-law review: **do not assume a broad non-reliance clause can eliminate fraud or statutory misleading-conduct exposure**.

## 3. Disclosure and Buyer knowledge: reject the blanket risk transfer  
**Schedule 7; clause 8.3; Disclosure Letter §§1.1–1.2**

General disclosure of the entire data room, documents “referred to” there, public records and everything advisers could have discovered is exceptionally broad. Coupled with the all-Claims limitations, it could make negotiated warranties largely ineffective.

**Push back:**
- Require **fair disclosure**, with sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the matter, linked to the relevant warranty.
- Reject indiscriminate incorporation of the data room and public registers. Any agreed general disclosures should be tightly defined.
- Freeze and retain an indexed, accessible copy of the disclosed materials at an agreed cutoff.
- Delete constructive knowledge and “discoverable” knowledge.
- If a knowledge limitation is unavoidable, restrict it to actual conscious knowledge of named Buyer deal-team members; exclude blanket imputation of advisers’ knowledge.
- Preserve specific indemnities and completion obligations notwithstanding disclosure or knowledge.
- Do not allow subsequent disclosures automatically to qualify warranties without Buyer agreement and corresponding remedies.

The Seller’s reservation that disclosure admits no breach does not resolve the underlying risk. Conversely, disclosure of uncertainty does not prove that a breach or loss exists.

## 4. Other material diligence and covenant issues

### Export/privacy incident  
**Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6; Disclosure Letter §6; DD-006**

The Seller’s “not expected to be material” characterisation is unsupported by the preliminary investigation. But the evidence also does **not** establish a confirmed notifiable breach.

Require investigation of access/download logs, containment, affected information and recipients, applicable privacy/security and contractual obligations, and notification requirements. Preserve evidence and require continuing updates and legally compliant remediation.

Negotiate a specific indemnity for attributable pre-Completion incident liabilities and reasonable investigation/remediation costs, including penalties only to the extent lawfully indemnifiable. Depending on findings, consider a completion condition or retention. Do not invent a loss amount.

### Sandbar renewals  
**Disclosure Letter §8; DD-008 / DD-011**

The **AUD 330,000 aggregate** should be evaluated together. Three AUD 110,000 contracts do not necessarily represent three independent ordinary-course decisions.

Check signing and renewal dates, scope, necessity, termination rights, accruals and compliance with interim operating covenants and commitment thresholds. Require Buyer approval where appropriate. **Do not automatically deduct ordinary future operating expenditure from price**, but capture any agreed Seller-borne, undisclosed or improperly incurred commitments.

### Lease and Mossvale  
**Disclosure Letter §§7–9; DD-007 / DD-009**

Avoid unsupported consent demands:
- The lease identifies a **notification** obligation: verify its timing and satisfy it.
- Mossvale’s assignment restriction does not, on the supplied wording, establish a consent requirement for a share sale.

Check the complete contracts for separate change-control provisions and consequences.

### Share title  
**Disclosure Letter §10; DD-012**

The register is evidence of recorded ownership, not a complete title diligence exercise. Verify issued capital, corporate records, transfer restrictions, options/convertibles, third-party interests and relevant security searches. Require valid transfers, necessary approvals, registration of the Buyer and release of share encumbrances, supported by robust fundamental warranties.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

1. **No unsecured completion gaps:** effective Bluefen consent, Riverlark repayment/release arrangements and verified IP ownership.
2. **Correct the economics:** capture debt, bonuses and applicable on-costs without double counting.
3. **Restore enforceable recourse:** reject all-Claims limitations and blanket disclosure/deemed knowledge.
4. **Separate fundamental, tax and known-risk protection** from the general warranty regime.
5. **Resolve uncertainty before accepting risk:** investigate the incident and supplier commitments; use conditions, specific indemnities and funded retentions where warranted.
6. **Check recoverability:** confirm the Seller’s ability to meet claims and negotiate escrow, retention or other security where necessary.

**Bottom line:** do not accept disclosure as a substitute for cure, price allocation or enforceable protection.
